# The Out-of-the-Loop Performance Problem and Level of Control in Automation

MICA R. ENDSLEY $^{1}$ and ESIN O. KIRIS, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas

The out-of-the-loop performance problem, a major potential consequence of automation, leaves operators of automated systems handicapped in their ability to take over manual operations in the event of automation failure. This is attributed to a possible loss of skills and of situation awareness (SA) arising from vigilance and complacency problems, a shift from active to passive information processing, and change in feedback provided to the operator. We studied the automation of a navigation task using an expert system and demonstrated that low SA corresponded with out-of-the-loop performance decrements in decision time following a failure of the expert system. Level of operator control in interacting with automation is a major factor in moderating this loss of SA. Results indicated that the shift from active to passive processing was most likely responsible for decreased SA under automated conditions.

## INTRODUCTION

The out-of-the-loop performance problem has been widely documented as a potential negative consequence of automation (Billings, 1991; Moray, 1986; Wickens, 1992; Wiener and Curry, 1980). System operators working with automation have been found to have a diminished ability both to detect system errors and subsequently to perform tasks manually in the face of automation failures, compared with operators who manually perform the same tasks. This paper will explore the possible etiologies of this phenomenon and potential means for ameliorating the problem.

The out-of-the-loop performance can be linked to two major issues associated with the implementation of automation: loss of manual skills and loss of awareness of the state and processes of the system.

## Loss of Skills

The loss of manual skills is a major concern accompanying the introduction of automation. Shiff (1983), for instance, found that despite initial manual training, those subjects who had been operating as supervisory controllers of automation in a simulated process control task were slower and more inefficient in bringing the system under control than were subjects who had operated only in a manual mode. Weiner and Curry (1980) cited concerns by aircraft flight crews that a loss of proficiency will occur with extensive use of automatic equipment. The fear is that manual skills will deteriorate with lack of use and flight crews will no longer be proficient at manual operations when needed. Wiener (1988) reported that in response to these concerns pilots are routinely operating in a manual mode in order to maintain flight skills.

There is also a concern that appropriate skills may not be developed if operators learn to operate with automated systems initially, without benefit of extensive manual experience. Moray (1986), building on the work of Rasmussen (1981, 1983) and Bainbridge (1981) discussed the need to provide operators with appropriate models. "If the operator has been trained exclusively for outer-loop control and is suddenly required to close an inner loop in an emergency when the automatic systems fail, this will be impossible" (Moray, 1986, p. 40/36). This has become a concern in automated aircraft, where new pilots may have little opportunity to acquire or practice manual skills or may not take full advantage of the opportunities they do have (Orlady and Wheeler, 1989).

These skills may be important not only for performing a task manually, but also for detecting the need for manual performance. In research relevant to this issue, Kessel and Wickens (1982) investigated the detection of system failures as evidenced by changes in dynamics associated with an automated tracking task. Although detection of changes in system dynamics in the manual mode was always superior to that in the automated mode, prior experience with operating in the manual mode led to superior performance in the automated mode when compared with the performance of subjects who had operated only with the system in the automated mode. Kessel and Wickens attributed this finding to the development of internal models when subjects were operating in the manual mode. These models directed subjects' attention to important cues that were also relevant in the automated mode. They did not find that internal models developed in the automated mode transferred to performance in the manual mode; those subjects performed significantly worse when switched to the manual mode. This finding supports the importance of manual experience in developing skills relevant to the detection of automation failures.

## Loss of Situation Awareness

It is the central thesis of this paper that a loss of situation awareness (SA) underlies a great deal of the out-of-the-loop performance problem (Endsley, 1987). Situation awareness is defined as “the perception of elements in the environment within a volume of time and space, the comprehension of their meaning, and the projection of their status in the near future” (Endsley, 1988, p. 97). As such, this includes an operator’s perception of relevant system state variables (Level 1 SA), an understanding of the meaning of that system state based on a synthesis of Level 1 data and in light of operator goals (Level 2 SA), and a projection of future trends and events in the system based on this understanding (Level 3 SA). Situation awareness is critical to effective decision making and human performance in dynamic systems (Endsley, 1993b).

A lack of situation awareness may be directly responsible for much of the out-of-the-loop performance decrement. Operators who have lost SA may be slower to detect problems and require extra time to reorient themselves to relevant system parameters in order to proceed with problem diagnosis and assumption of manual performance. Evidence for this assertion can be categorized into three major areas: (1) a loss of vigilance and increase in complacency associated with the assumption of a monitoring role; (2) a move from active processor of information to passive recipient of information, and (3) a loss of or change in the type of feedback provided to operators concerning the state of the system.

Vigilance, complacency, and monitoring. A long history denotes a lack of operator awareness of automation failures and a decrease in detection of critical system state changes when operating in an automated mode. Working with early efforts at automating flight tasks, Wempe (1965) found that pilots were unaware of autopilot disconnects. Billings (1991) reported on various aircraft accidents in which problems in monitoring automation occurred, concluding that the probability of occurrence increases (a) when devices behave reasonably but incorrectly and (b) when pilots are not alert to the state of automation.

Although vigilance problems have normally been associated with simple, low-workload tasks, Parasuraman (1987) reviewed vigilance problems associated with complex tasks. He concluded that “vigilance effects can be found in complex monitoring and that humans may be poor passive monitors of an automated system, irrespective of the complexity of events being monitored” (p. 703). Several studies have found inferior failure detection performance to be associated with operators of automated systems (Ephrath and Young, 1981; Kessel and Wickens, 1982; Wickens and Kessel, 1979; Young, 1969). Factors such as the automation’s detection criterion point, the attention demands of other tasks, and the way in which the human and automation are coupled appear to affect this issue (Parasuraman, 1987).

Complacency has been cited as a major factor associated with lack of vigilance in monitoring under automation. Bergeron (1981) noted that pilots working with increased levels of automation in an autopilot were more likely to lose track of where they were. This was at least partially attributed to complacency, which allowed the pilots to become absorbed in other tasks. Problems associated with complacency have been attributed to the tendency of human controllers to place too much trust in automated systems (Danaher, 1980; Parasuraman, Molloy, and Singh, 1993; Wiener, 1985). Singh, Molloy, and Parasuraman (1993) found that complacency potential was a function of a person's trust in, reliance on, and confidence in automation. "Devices that are extremely reliable will come, over time, to be relied upon by pilots. In the rare cases when they fail, or are disabled, pilots may not be sufficiently able to detect the condition for which the device was originally provided. This occurred in two recent attempted takeoffs with flaps and leading edge devices retracted. The aircraft crashed with heavy loss of life" (Billings, 1991, p. 38).

Wiener (1985) reported that pilots attributed their own complacency to the fact that the equipment was so reliable. Lee and Moray (1992) explicitly investigated the role of trust in human performance with automated systems, where trust was defined as a function of predictability, dependability, and faith in the system. They found a significant and dramatic impact of system faults on operator trust that was related to the magnitude of the fault and which had a continued impact on future trials with a slow, gradual regaining of trust. Performance was similarly affected, although operators were largely able to compensate for system faults with altered control strategies.

Recent research by Parasuraman et al. (1993) investigated the effects of system reliability on operator detection of system failures. They found that although the mean level of automation reliability was not related to failure detection performance, the variability associated with automation reliability was. Performance effects associated with complacency were likely to be observed only in multitask environments, however, and not when the operator's sole task was to monitor the automation.

A lack of vigilance has also been associated with systems with a high incidence of false alarms, leading to a lack of trust in the automation. Wiener and Curry (1980) and Billings (1991) reported on many failures by aircrews to heed automatic alarms, which led to serious accidents. Even though in such cases the system provides a clear visual or auditory signal, it is ignored or disabled by flight crew who have no faith in the system because of its high false alarm rate.

Active versus passive. Increased latency in detecting system problems has been discussed in relation to a lack of vigilance and complacency. In addition, the fact that operators are passive instead of active processors of information may add to their problems in detecting the need for manual intervention and in reorienting themselves to the state of the system in order to do so. Evidence suggests that passive processing of information may be inferior to active processing (Cowan, 1988; Slamecka and Graf, 1978). This factor could make a dynamic update of system information and integration of that information in active working memory less attainable under passive conditions.

Feedback. A change in the type of system feedback or a complete loss of feedback has also been frequently cited. "Without appropriate feedback, people are indeed out of the loop: They may not know if their requests have been received, if the actions are being performed properly, or if problems are occurring" (Norman, 1989, p. 6).

In many cases, certain critical cues may be eliminated with automation and replaced by other cues that do not result in the same level of performance. Young (1969) reported that hand movement information was important for detecting changes in system dynamics associated with a tracking task and that this is denied in an automated situation. Kessel and Wickens (1982) felt that the fact that subjects operating under automation had only visual cues, whereas subjects in a manual condition had both visual and proprioceptive information, was significant to their findings, particularly if the cues conflicted. De Keyser (as reported in Moray, 1986) cited the heavy use process control operators make of informal information such as vibration and smell. "The removal of operators from physical contact with the process may impoverish their diagnostic environment despite the more sophisticated displays" (Moray, 1986, p. 40/38).

In some cases the design of the automated system intentionally occludes information from the operator. Displays associated with many systems eliminate raw system data in favor of processed, integrated information. When the presented information is incorrect, “the clarity and apparent precision of the displays can be seductive” (Billings, 1991, p. 37). Information overload associated with presenting too much information can also act to obscure needed information, leading to a loss of situation awareness. Billings also reported on several aircraft accidents associated with autofeathering systems, which do not notify pilots of their actions in shutting down engines. The system design does not provide sufficient information to keep the pilot aware of system actions.

Norman (1989) cited several cases of automation-related accidents in which adequate feedback was not provided. He attributed this largely to the belief by system designers that information on system status is no longer needed by system operators once relevant functions are assumed by automation. Serious errors occur when the automation fails, however, as the system does not provide the operator with the needed information to detect this occurrence and take over manual control. Providing adequate feedback under automation to keep the operator informed, yet not overloaded, may be a formidable challenge for designers of future systems.

## Benefits to SA

It should be noted that automation does not always result in these types of problems. Curry and Ephrath (1977) found that monitors of an automatic system actually performed better than manual controllers in a flight task. They attributed this to the fact that, as monitors, subjects were able to better distribute their attention across other displays that helped in detecting system failures, whereas, when functioning as manual controllers, they needed to devote their attention to a narrower range of cues. Wiener (1992) pointed out that situation awareness may be enhanced with automated systems, which can provide superior, integrated information to operators. He also stressed the fact that automation has, by and large, worked quite well and has accompanied a dramatic reduction in many types of human errors (Wiener, 1985).

In addition, automation may improve situation awareness by reducing excessive workload. "Automation can lighten this burden on pilots, first by relieving them of the burden of inner-loop control, second by providing integrated information, and third by allowing them to manage at a higher level" (Billings, 1991, p. 17). Whether automation actually results in lower workload, however, remains questionable (Wiener, 1985). Bainbridge (1983) has noted that when workload is the highest, automation is often of the least assistance, as it usually can handle only routine tasks. Furthermore, recent research has demonstrated a certain degree of independence between SA and workload (Endsley, 1993a), indicating that even if workload is successfully reduced, this may not translate into higher SA.

## Level of Control

Much of the research on out-of-the-loop performance has focused on the automation of psychomotor manual control tasks. Automation is being increasingly applied to higher-level decision tasks in the form of artificial intelligence (AI) or expert systems. The technical and practical considerations associated with achieving a successful implementation of AI in various complex systems have been widely discussed (Ignizio, 1991; Waterman, 1986); however, a major issue still to be dealt with is the impact that automation of cognitive tasks may have on an operator's situation awareness and ability to respond in the event of system breakdowns or inadequacies.

In order to realize any positive benefits of automating cognitive tasks, the potential negative effects must be avoided by discovering a method of keeping the operator actively involved in the decision-making loop while simultaneously reducing the load associated with doing everything manually. It has been proposed that this can be accomplished by determining a level of automation that will minimize negative effects on operator situation awareness (Endsley, 1987, 1992).

Wiener and Curry (1980) and Billings (1991) have discussed the fact that automation does not exist in an all-or-none fashion but can be implemented at various levels. In relation to this discussion, a task may be accomplished (a) manually, with no assistance from the system; (b) by the operator, with input in the form of recommendations provided by the system; (c) by the system, with the consent of the operator required to carry out the action; (d) by the system, to be automatically implemented unless vetoed by the operator; or (e) fully automatically, with no operator interaction (Endsley, 1987, 1992). These five possible levels of automation, from none to full, are depicted in Figure 1.

In order to investigate the hypothesis that the level of automation can have a significant impact on the out-of-the-loop performance problem and to experimentally verify the role of situation awareness in this process, a study was conducted in which a cognitive task was automated via a simulated expert system.

## METHODOLOGY

## Experimental Design

The experiment was constructed as a between-subjects design. The primary independent variable was the level of control established between the subject and the system: (a) manual, in which the subject acts alone with no expert system (control condition); (b) decision support, in which the subject acts using recommendations from the system; (c) consensual AI, in which the system acts with subject concurrence required; (d) monitored AI, in which the system acts with subject veto possible; and (e) full automation, in which the system acts completely automatically with no human intervention possible.

The dependent measures included time for subjects to make a decision when an expert system breakdown was simulated, the decision selected, subject confidence about the correctness of decisions made, workload, and situation awareness. Subject decision time was measured to the nearest thousandth of a second by the computer's clock. Subject confidence level was obtained as a subjective estimate, on a scale from 1 to 10. Subject workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX standardized subjective workload scale (Hart and Staveland, 1988).

Subject situation awareness was assessed using seven queries designed to evaluate the subject's knowledge of actions taken during the automated portion of the task.

## Task

The task was implemented using Hypercard software running on a Macintosh computer. An automobile navigation task was created that depicted a real-world driving situation, adapted from Selcon (1990). An example scenario is shown in Figure 2. For each of six scenarios, a paragraph of text describing a decision task was presented. An expert system was simulated that provided three decision options and the probability that each was the correct solution to the problem. After reading the problem description, the subjects called up the list of decision options, which was displayed under the problem paragraph, adjacent to the system's assigned probabilities. Subjects were instructed to select the option they considered the most likely to be correct as quickly and accurately as possible. They were given one practice trial.

The subject's task varied in each experimental condition.

(1) Manual. The subject's task was to observe the presented scenarios and decide on one of the three possible actions. Expert system probabilities assigned to each alternative were not presented in this condition; however, all other information on the three alternatives was presented. After subjects selected an option by clicking the mouse on its associated button, the next scenario was presented.

(2) Decision support. The subject's task was to observe the presented scenarios and the expert system's recommendations, represented as probabilities associated with each alternative, and then decide on one of the three possible actions. (Subjects were free to select any alternative; however, previous research indicates that alternatives other than that with the highest probability of being correct are selected only approximately 9% of the time on this task [Kiris and Endsley, 1993].) After subjects selected an option, the next scenario was presented.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2. Example scenario.

(3) Consensual AI. The subject's task was the same as in the decision support condition; however, in this condition the expert system also selected one of the options by highlighting the button associated with the highest-probability alternative. The subject could either concur with this choice by selecting the OK button or select another alternative by designating it.

(4) Monitored AI. This condition was similar to the consensual AI condition; however, in this condition the system would also implement its selected alternative unless the subject vetoed the system's recommendation within 30 s and selected a different alternative. (Based on previous research, 30 s was deemed sufficient time for most subjects to make a selection when operating in a manual mode [Kiris and Endsley, 1993].)

(5) Full automation. In this condition the system acted in an automatic fashion, with the subject completely out of the loop. The subject could observe the system's selection for 30 s before the next scenario was presented. No action was possible by the subjects in this condition—they were strictly monitors.

In all four of the conditions employing the expert system, system breakdown occurred after the fourth scenario, placing the subject in a purely manual condition for the fifth and sixth scenarios. The only difference among conditions in these scenarios, therefore, was the level of control exerted prior to the system breakdown. Subjects' manual performance on the decision tasks in Scenarios 5 and 6, which occurred after the automation breakdown, can therefore be examined as a function of the level of automation prior to the breakdown (the issue of interest in this study). System breakdown was clearly indicated by a visual message at the bottom of the screen and the absence of system-generated probabilities or alternative selection. Subjects were informed prior to beginning the session that they would need to perform the task un-aided should the system break down.

Subjects' confidence in their decisions was elicited at the end of the fifth and sixth scenarios. Following the scenarios, subjective workload was elicited using an on-screen version of NASA-TLX. Seven situation awareness queries were then administered. Four of these addressed knowledge of specific actions taken during the first four scenarios, which would correspond to Level 1 SA, and three addressed subjects' understanding of actions taken in regard to the navigation task, which would correspond to Level 2 SA.

## Subjects

Eighty undergraduate students (64 male, 16 female) at Texas Tech University participated on voluntary basis for extra credit in a course. Subjects' mean age was 22.9 years with a variance of 9.5. Sixteen subjects participated in each condition, using a between-subjects design.

## Hypotheses

It was hypothesized that subjects' mental workload and situation awareness level would decrease with increasing levels of automation (or decreasing levels of control). Corresponding with this decrease in SA, it was expected that subjects' decision time in the scenarios after system breakdown would increase with increasing levels of automation (decreasing levels of control) experienced prior to the expert system breakdown. It was also hypothesized that subjects' confidence in making decisions after the breakdown would decrease with increasing levels of automation (decreasing levels of control) experienced prior to the expert system breakdown, as they would feel less skilled.

## RESULTS

## Analysis of Response Time

The mean decision time of the subjects in each of the five conditions is plotted in Figure 3 across the six scenarios of the experiment. Under full automation the decision time was constant at 30 s, as determined by the system. Although subjects in the monitored AI condition could have manually selected an alternative and proceeded to the next scenario sooner, most frequently they appeared to allow the system to proceed to the next scenario after the 30 s had elapsed. Subjects in the consensual AI and decision support conditions had slightly faster mean decision times than the unaided subjects.

Of primary interest from the standpoint of this study are Scenarios 5 and 6, which reflect manual decision times after the automation failed. Results of an analysis of variance (ANOVA) for decision time in the final two scenarios showed a significant effect of condition, $F(4,150) = 2.58$, $p < 0.05$ ($\beta = 0.26$), and scenario, $F(1,150) = 40.88$, $p < 0.01$ ($\beta < 0.01$), but not a condition-by-scenario interaction ($\beta < 0.01$). Decisions in the fifth scenario, immediately following the system breakdown, always took longer than in the sixth scenario, across all conditions. Corresponding with the hypothesized effect, decisions following the system breakdown took longer for subjects who had been under higher levels of automation. A Tukey comparison test showed only the manual and fully automated conditions to be significantly different, however (p < 0.05).

## Analysis of Confidence Level

Results of an ANOVA for confidence level also showed a significant effect of condition,  $F(4,149) = 2.48$ , p < 0.05 ( $\beta = 0.30$ ), but not of scenario ( $\beta > 0.60$ ) or a condition-by-scenario interaction ( $\beta = 0.45$ ). Mean confidence level combined across the two scenarios is depicted in Figure 4. Contrary to the hypothesis, subjects were more confident about their decisions when they had been operating with expert system assistance. A Tukey comparison test showed that confidence level was significantly higher in the monitored AI condition than in the manual condition but that it was not significantly different among the other three conditions (p < 0.05). Although not statistically different, confidence level also appeared higher in all of the automated conditions than in the manual condition.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 3. Mean decision time by level of automation.

## Analysis of Situation Awareness

Subjects' answers to the situation awareness queries were scored as correct or incorrect, based on what had happened in the scenarios. SA Level 1 and SA Level 2 scores were calculated as percentage correct for the questions in each category. An arcsine transformation was applied in order to meet the conditions for performing analysis of variance.

Level 1 SA was not significantly different among the conditions based on an ANOVA ( $\beta = 0.58$ ). Level 2 SA was significantly different among the conditions, however,  $F(4,75) = 2.54$ , p < 0.05 ( $\beta = 0.30$ ). This is shown in Figure 5. Subjects had poorer SA (more incorrect answers) at the end of the trial when they had been acting in the fully automatic condition than when they had been in the manual condition (p < 0.05). The intermediate levels of automation corresponded to an intermediate level of SA.

## Analysis of Workload

Subjects' ratings of workload on each of the NASA-TLX dimensions were weighted based on their rankings of dimensions obtained at the end of each experimental session to obtain a single workload score for each subject. Results of an ANOVA did not show a significant effect of condition on subjective workload ( $\beta > 0.60$ ).

## Analysis of Options Selected

Overall, subjects were not more likely to have made different decisions in the different conditions, either before or after the expert system breakdown, based on chi-square tests at a 0.05 level of significance. The alternative with the highest probability was selected 95% of the time before the automation failure and 94% of the time after the automation failure across all conditions. Even when operating in a fully manual mode (without knowledge of the probabilities assigned to alternatives), correct decisions were usually made, although they took longer on average than when assistance was provided through decision support or consensual AI.

## DISCUSSION

The out-of-the-loop performance problem was demonstrated in this study utilizing a high-level cognitive task. Operators were slower to perform the task manually following the breakdown of the automated system than if they had been performing manually all along. This effect appears to have been more severe under full automation than under the partial automation conditions. A corresponding decrease in situation awareness accompanied this shift, supporting the major hypothesized relationship between these two factors.

Figure 5. Level 2 situation awareness across levels of automation.

It is interesting that only Level 2 SA—understanding of the situation—was affected by automation level. Although subjects were monitoring the system, as reflected by Level 1 SA scores, they may not have developed the higher-level understanding of the situation reflected in the Level 2 queries under the automated conditions. In these conditions, subjects were not required to work through the problem scenarios on their own, given that they could rely on the expert system. This is particularly worrisome, as it is this higher level understanding of system state that is crucial for effective problem detection, diagnosis, and control (Endsley, 1993b). Recent research by Carmody and Gluckman (1993) found similar results, with Level 2 (but not Level 1) SA lower under fully automated conditions.

It is also interesting that workload was not reduced by the automated assistance provided, even under full automation. This is in line with previous assertions that automation may not actually reduce workload but, rather, shift the type of workload as a greater monitoring load is incurred (Billings, 1991; Wiener, 1985).

Although confidence level was expected to be lower under the automated conditions, the reverse was actually the case. Subjects who had previously had expert system assistance were more confident of their ability to make decisions manually than were subjects who had been operating manually all along. It is possible that subjects who had been observing the expert system's results felt that they had gleaned useful knowledge about solving the navigation problems, thus raising their confidence in their own problem-solving abilities. No data were collected to test this assertion, however. In any event, there did not appear to be any perceived loss of skills that resulted in lower confidence.

No objective loss of skills was detected, either; subjects were just as likely to select the optimum choice after the system breakdown, regardless of their prior automation condition. In fact, selection of either of the nonoptimal alternatives was very low in all conditions, both before and after the breakdown.

## Theoretical Implications

It could be argued that the poorer manual performance exhibited by subjects who had been operating under automated conditions reflects a lack of practice in performing the decision tasks, leading to differences among the subject groups, primarily in skill. The lower level of SA possessed by these subjects, however, clearly indicates that this explanation alone is not sufficient for explaining the data. Not only were subjects slower in performing tasks manually when they had previously been under moderate and high levels of automation, but they were also less aware of what had been happening. This, of course, demonstrates only a casual and not a causal relationship between SA and the out-of-the-loop performance problem; however, the finding is significant. No theoretical link can be drawn between SA decrements and the out-of-the-loop performance problem if it arises purely from a lack of skills. The fact that subjects were more confident of their manual performance when they had been operating in the automated conditions and were just as likely to select the “best” alternative as the other subjects also lends credence to the rejection of an explanation based purely on skill.

The importance of situation awareness in the out-of-the-loop performance problem can therefore be concluded from these data. A loss of situation awareness accompanying increased levels of automation was hypothesized to occur through (a) problems with vigilance and complacency, (b) lack of active information processing, and (c) reduced or altered feedback on system state. In this particular task, it is very unlikely that the last issue came into play. Information presentation was identical in all conditions.

It is also unlikely that actual vigilance problems were encountered. The total time for task performance was approximately 10 min per subject. In addition, the automation of only a single task was involved. Neither Thackray and Touchstone (1989) nor Parasuraman et al. (1993) found complacency effects when subjects monitored only a single automated task. These effects were encountered only when a second task was involved (Parasuraman et al., 1993). In addition, it would be expected that if less attention had been directed to the task under the automated condition because of lack of monitoring, Level 1 SA would have decreased as well as Level 2 SA. This was not the case, however.

It would seem most likely, therefore, that the loss of SA experienced under the automated conditions was attributable to the difference between active and passive processing of information. As would be expected, this affected Level 2 SA (understanding) more than Level 1 SA (perception). This is not to say that SA losses attributable to vigilance, complacency, or lack of feedback do not occur. Indeed, the research reviewed earlier would strongly suggest that they do. Merely, it appears that these factors were not the primary culprits in this study, highlighting the importance of the shift from active to passive decision making that occurs when automation is implemented. This issue has not received much explicit consideration in research and needs to be addressed in future studies.

## Design Implications

As the tasks becoming automated fall increasingly into the cognitive domain, the shift from active to passive processing under automation may become particularly troublesome. Although the task in this study was a fairly simple navigation task, similar performance problems with more complex cognitive tasks under automated conditions have been noted. Shiff's (1983) study of process controllers revealed relatively poor performance in bringing the system under control when switching from fully automated conditions to manual control. In his seminal work on flexible manufacturing systems, Sharit (1985) found that when human controllers freely intervened with an automated system, performance on numerous system parameters was poorer than that of the automated system acting alone. This was the case even with various forms of feedback studied.

Currently, it is being proposed that AI systems be implemented in cockpits and advanced air traffic control systems with the idea that human pilots and controllers will be able to oversee these systems and take over when necessary. This research points to the fact that they may not be able to do so adequately, however, as their SA may be compromised by their passive role in the processing of information. Clearly, there are serious problems involved in integrating humans and automation of complex cognitive tasks that need to be resolved.

Although a more linear, negative relationship between increasing levels of automation and both performance and SA were expected, this study did find that full automation produced more problems than did partial automation, which in turn produced more problems than the manual condition. There did appear to be an ameliorating effect, observable in both SA and decision time data, introduced by the use of lower levels of automation, which maintained a higher level of control for the operator. A partial automation strategy may therefore be indicated in designing automation so as to avoid some of the negative consequences associated with out-of-the-loop performance.

## Further Research

This research looked only at automation involving a high-level cognitive task. Further research is needed to examine other types of tasks, which may involve different types of SA and workload trade-offs with varied levels of control. Psychomotor tasks, for instance, may act to subtly transmit information important for SA, which may be jeopardized by automation schemes that decrease this type of input even though workload might also be decreased.

Other automation aids act to enhance perceptually presented data (through data fusion, for instance) or directly affect attention, such as aircraft conflict detection alerts. Theoretically these forms of automation will reduce attention and workload requirements while presenting SA-oriented information and thus should benefit SA through full automation. Any lesser level of automation may unnecessarily tie up the operator's attention without benefiting SA. The main danger of full automation of these tasks could come from overreliance on the system.

The impact of automation on cognitive tasks may also depend on the type of task being automated. Routine, repetitive, and peripheral tasks, such as mental calculations and integration, should benefit from full automation by providing workload reduction while creating information at the level needed for SA. Cognitive tasks that are central to the operators' decision-making goals, such as the one in this study, should benefit from an intermediate level of automation, which keeps the operator involved in the decision loop. Research is needed to examine these possibilities before firm conclusions can be drawn regarding the best level of automation to use for a task.

## CONCLUSION

As both SA and decision time following system breakdown were negatively affected in this study without any reduction in workload, it may be asked whether automation should be implemented at all, echoing earlier concerns (Wiener and Curry, 1980). As Billings (1991) pointed out, this question is nearly academic, as fully automated systems are currently being introduced in air transport and many other types of systems.

It may be more appropriate instead to determine implementation methods that minimize negative effects while maintaining the benefits of automation. This research suggests that implementing automation while maintaining a high level of control for the human operator provides definite benefits in minimizing the out-of-the-loop performance problem, as compared with full automation. Recent work by Parasuraman (1992) found improvements in system failure detection by having operators assume manual control at periodic intervals. More work is needed to explore techniques such as these in order to establish human-centered automation that maximizes overall human-system performance.
